I am not arguing for inaction. I am arguing for proportion, and for honesty with the public. If we tell people that the burden falls on them while the largest emitters carry on untouched, we will lose their consent, and once consent is lost on a question like this it is extremely hard to win back. A carbon tax without an alternative is simply a tax. It becomes a climate measure only when the person paying it has somewhere else to go. In my constituency there are towns where the last evening bus leaves at six o'clock. There are households retrofitting nothing because the grant covers a fraction of the cost and the balance is beyond them. There are farmers being told to cut the herd with no clear account of what replaces that income. Meanwhile we import beef from countries clearing forest to produce it and count none of that against ourselves. What I want is straightforward. Ring-fence the revenue and return it in a way people can actually see on a statement. Deliver retrofitting at a scale that reaches low income homes rather than those who could have afforded the work anyway. Invest seriously in rural transport before rural drivers are penalised. And argue Ireland's case internationally with the same energy the Government applies to lecturing its own citizens. Do those things and I will support the measures and defend them publicly. Continue as we are and the Government will find that the public turns against the entire climate project, which would be the worst outcome available to us and the hardest to undo.

Every time members opposite suggest they would tear up these agreements, they raise the cost of capital for every project in the country. Is there more to do? Of course there is. The transition has to reach the communities that depended on the internal combustion supply chain, and it has to reach them before the plants close rather than afterwards. Some students lost weeks of contact time. Some had no quiet place to study and no reliable broadband. Some were caring for relatives or working to support a household. If we run the papers as though none of that happened, the results will reflect household circumstances as much as ability, and the students hurt worst will be the ones already furthest behind. So the adjustments matter, and so does the contingency. I have asked officials to have an alternative pathway ready in detail, not in outline, in the event that public health makes examinations impossible. I would rather prepare something we never use than improvise in June. I want to say one more thing to students directly, because I know some of them are listening. It could include work with religious leaders who hold real authority locally and who, when they choose to, take considerable personal risk to speak against violence. It could include trauma healing and reconciliation work, which is slow and unglamorous and rarely produces a photograph for a Minister to stand in front of, but which determines whether a ceasefire holds five years later. It could include the practical business of getting rival groups into a room, feeding them, and keeping them talking long enough for something to shift. Faith organisations are often uniquely placed to do this because they are already there. They were there before the crisis, they stay through it, and they will be there long after the international agencies have moved on to the next emergency. They have networks no external actor can replicate and a legitimacy that cannot be purchased. That is exactly why we should think carefully about how we fund them. If we treat these organisations as delivery contractors and load them with reporting requirements designed for large international NGOs, we will exclude the very local partners whose involvement makes the work effective. I have asked officials to look again at the accessibility of our funding streams for smaller faith-based and community organisations, including the minimum grant size and the language in which applications must be submitted. I would also say to the House that peacebuilding is not a soft alternative to security policy. It is considerably cheaper than the alternative, and the evidence base for it has improved substantially over the last decade. Every conflict we help to prevent is a humanitarian appeal we do not have to launch and a stabilisation deployment we do not have to fund. I hope that when the strategy is published, my hon. Friend will find that argument reflected in it rather than confined to the annexes.

The framework it establishes is a genuine improvement and I do not want the perfect to be the enemy of the good. But let me put on the record what I will be watching for. I want the implementation timelines published and adhered to. I want the funding attached, because a right without resources is a press release. I want reporting done in a form communities themselves can scrutinize, rather than buried in a departmental annual report nobody reads. And I want to see what happens the first time a community uses the powers in this bill to reach a conclusion the government finds inconvenient. That will tell us whether any of this means anything, and I suspect we will find out sooner than the minister expects.

I do not think this is a partisan matter and I do not think anyone here is indifferent to victims. But the system we have built treats the victim as a witness to a dispute between the Crown and the accused, and once the trial ends their standing largely evaporates. They have to apply to be informed. They have to register, and then re-register. They find out where the offender is being held, often, from a journalist. In the case raised repeatedly in this House, the family learned of a transfer from the media. Whatever one's view of the correctional decision itself, that is indefensible as a matter of basic decency, and it is entirely within the power of this Parliament to fix. What I would like to see is straightforward. Notification should be automatic and opt-out rather than opt-in. Where a decision is made to move an offender to a lower security setting, the reasons should be recorded in language the family can actually read. Victim statements should follow the file rather than being submitted once and forgotten. And there should be somebody whose job it is to answer the phone when a family calls, because at present they are passed between three agencies, none of which considers itself responsible. None of this requires us to abandon rehabilitation, which I support and which the evidence supports. None of it requires longer sentences. It requires us to treat the people who were harmed as participants in the process rather than as an inconvenience to be managed once the sentencing hearing is over, and I would welcome the government moving on it in this Parliament rather than the next.

my own county the local authority once ran the housing programme, the water services, the roads, the fire service and a good deal besides, and it did so with staff who lived in the communities they served and who could be stopped in the street and asked a question. Successive reorganisations have stripped functions away, centralised them into national agencies, and left the elected member with a great deal of responsibility and almost no power. That is a bad combination. It produces frustration among councillors, confusion among the public about who is actually accountable, and decisions taken at a remove from the places they affect. If this Bill is to mean anything it has to reverse some of that, and reversing it requires two things that are not in the Bill as drafted. The first is money the local authority controls itself, rather than allocations from the centre with conditions attached down to the last line item. An authority that cannot raise or retain a meaningful share of its own revenue is an administrative office, not a government. The second is staff. We can transfer functions all day long, but if the sanction to recruit sits centrally then the function arrives without the capacity to discharge it, and in two years we will be back here discussing why delivery has been poor. Councils in my part of the country cannot recruit engineers or planners because they cannot compete on pay with the agencies, let alone the private sector, and we have critical posts advertised three times over. I would also raise the executive-elected balance. A chief executive can in practice decline to act on the settled will of the members across a wide range of matters. I understand the history behind that and I am not naive about why it was introduced, but it has gone too far, and the people who face the electorate should be able to direct the organisation they were elected to lead.

We have reflected on that feedback and I am bringing forward amendments today which I hope address it. The concern was essentially that the removal provisions as originally drafted gave insufficient clarity about the grounds on which an arbitrator could be removed and about who bore the cost of any consequent rehearing. That is a legitimate concern. If parties cannot predict the circumstances in which a tribunal might be reconstituted, the process loses the speed and certainty that is its principal advantage over litigation, and we would have created a scheme nobody uses. The amendments therefore do three things. They set out the grounds for removal exhaustively rather than illustratively. They require the approving body to give written reasons, which brings the decision within the ordinary scope of review. And they make clear that where removal occurs for reasons unconnected with the conduct of either party, the costs of any consequential steps do not fall on the parties. I am grateful to the Institution and to the other professional bodies who engaged with officials on the drafting, and I want to record that their input improved the Bill. This is a good illustration of why pre-legislative engagement matters. These are technical provisions that will be operated by practitioners rather than by Ministers, and the people who will operate them are far better placed than we are to spot the point at which a well-intentioned clause becomes unworkable. Where we have not been able to accept a suggestion, officials have written to explain why, and I am content to place that correspondence in the Library. There remain one or two areas where views differ, in particular on the appointment mechanism and on the treatment of multi-party disputes, and I expect we will return to those in Committee. I would rather have that argument now than discover the difficulty in the first contested case.

At present, when a device is withdrawn, the process of identifying who has one is slow, manual, and in some cases simply impossible, because the record exists only in a hospital's own system and sometimes only on paper. I want to be clear with the House about the privacy dimension, because Members will have concerns and they are legitimate ones. This is sensitive information about people's bodies. The safeguards are that access is restricted to specified purposes, that those purposes appear on the face of the Bill rather than being left to regulations, and that extending them requires the affirmative procedure. I have deliberately resisted requests to include a research access gateway here. There is a strong case for such a gateway and I expect we will return to it, but it should be debated on its own terms rather than carried in behind a patient safety measure. The second use, which subsection (6) anticipates, is signal detection: noticing that a particular device is failing at an unusual rate before the individual failures are reported as such. That is where the real gain lies, and it is only achievable if the underlying data is complete, which is why compliance cannot be optional.

I do not want to be standing here in three years describing another such sequence. So I say to the Government that the measures announced are a start and only a start. The people around this regime hold assets in our jurisdiction, educate their children here, litigate here, and launder their reputations through our courts and our public relations industry. Every one of those is a point of leverage we have chosen not to use. The register of overseas entities has been promised for years. Reform of Companies House has been promised for years. Unexplained wealth orders have been used a handful of times because the costs risk makes enforcement agencies unwilling to act. These are not difficult problems. They are problems we have declined to solve because solving them imposes costs on people with influence in this country. That has to change now, and not after the next outrage.

self-employment. That conclusion came from a review this Government itself commissioned, and it has sat on a shelf since. The consequence is a labour market in which two people can do identical work, side by side, on the same site, with completely different rights, different tax treatment and different security, purely because of how the paperwork was drawn up. The person on the worse end of that arrangement almost never chose it. I meet these workers constantly. Delivery drivers told they are running their own business who cannot set their price, choose their route or refuse a job without penalty. Care workers on contracts that pay for the visit but not the travel between visits, so the effective hourly rate falls below the minimum wage and everyone involved knows it. Construction workers registered through intermediaries they have never dealt with directly. This is not a marginal phenomenon at the edge of the economy. It is a substantial and growing share of the labour market, and it grows because it is cheaper. That was the review's central finding. As long as an employer can cut its national insurance bill by reclassifying a worker, some employers will do it, and those who do not will be undercut by those who do. Decent employers lose that race, and I hear from them as often as I hear from the workers themselves. So we would legislate for a single status of worker with a clear statutory test, we would put the burden of proof on the engager rather than on the individual, and we would align the tax treatment so the incentive disappears. That last element is the hard one, and it is precisely why nothing has happened for five years. But avoiding it does not make it go away. It simply transfers the cost onto people who cannot afford to bear it.

What the federal government can do, and is doing through the housing accelerator, is make its money conditional on those rules changing. I would have preferred that lever pulled harder and earlier, and I have said so. Trust in this House on housing is close to exhausted, and it is exhausted for a straightforward reason: targets have been announced, missed, restated and missed again, and the people waiting have watched the whole cycle from a bedroom in their parents' house. I meet them every week. Nurses in their thirties who cannot rent within an hour of the hospital where they work. Families in emergency accommodation who have been there long enough that the children have changed school twice. People who did everything they were told to do and who now believe, with some justification, that the system was not built with them in mind. So when I say we must deliver what is promised in the budget, I mean the specific things. The social housing units must be built and not merely acquired from the market, because acquisition moves a family into a home without adding a home. The cost rental programme must scale beyond the pilot stage, and the rents must actually be affordable to somebody on the median income rather than affordable in a technical sense relative to a market that is itself broken. The vacancy measures must be enforced, which means resourcing local authorities to identify and pursue derelict property, not just legislating for a levy nobody collects. And the capacity constraints have to be faced honestly. We do not have the tradespeople. We have not had them since the last collapse drove a generation of them abroad, and the apprenticeship pipeline is not producing them fast enough. That is a solvable problem but only if it is treated as urgent now, because a target for 2030 depends on people who need to start training this year. I will support the measures that do this. They did not vote to remain subject to rules made in a room they are not in, and they certainly did not vote for the arrangement now being described, which appears to leave us with the obligations of membership and none of the influence. I recognise the difficulty the Government faces and I do not underestimate it. The border on the island of Ireland is a genuine problem, not a manufactured one, and anybody who pretends otherwise has not thought about it seriously. But I do not accept that the only available answer is an indefinite arrangement from which we cannot exit unilaterally. Every trade agreement in the world has a termination clause. The suggestion that this one uniquely cannot is a political choice being presented as a legal necessity. The compromise on the table has the merit of being supported across a range of opinion in this House, which is more than can be said for anything else that has been proposed in the last two years. It offers a defined transition, it offers time to develop the technical arrangements at the border, and it accepts that if those arrangements cannot be made to work, we manage that consequence rather than pre-emptively surrendering to avoid it. The question is about what happened before it was exercised. The principle at stake here is not obscure or technical. Prosecutorial independence exists because the alternative is a system in which the well-connected receive different treatment from everybody else. It is not a convention we invented recently. It is one of the oldest protections in our legal tradition and it survives precisely because governments of every stripe have accepted the constraint even when it was inconvenient to them. If it can be set aside because the economic consequences of a prosecution are judged to be significant, then it does not exist, because the economic consequences of prosecuting a large employer are always significant. That is the entire point. So what the committee needs is straightforward. A full waiver, so that all relevant testimony can be given without qualification. Access to the documentary record. Where asylum seekers are permitted to work after a short period, the labour market participation of those eventually granted status is markedly higher, dependence on state support is lower, and there is no detectable effect on the volume of applications. The pull-factor argument has been tested repeatedly and it does not survive the testing. People flee because of what is behind them, and the research on decision-making at the point of departure is consistent on this: the vast majority know almost nothing about the destination country's welfare rules. What the prohibition on work actually produces is well documented. It produces skill atrophy, so that a doctor who arrives at forty is unemployable at forty-three. It produces mental ill health, because enforced idleness combined with uncertainty is corrosive in a way anyone who has been long-term unemployed will recognise. It produces destitution, and where it produces destitution it produces illegal work, which is unregulated, unsafe and untaxed, and which undercuts the wages of people already here. The Deputy asked specifically about the political dialogue and cooperation agreement. The evidence now supports designated visitor arrangements with testing and protective equipment, and the professional bodies have said so. Yet the practice varies enormously between homes, and the variation is not explained by outbreak status. It is explained by the risk appetite of individual managers, who have been given guidance that is permissive but not directive, and who reasonably fear being blamed for an outbreak more than they fear the harm of continued isolation, because one of those harms produces an inspection and the other does not. That asymmetry is what the Minister must fix. Make the designated visitor a resident's right rather than a manager's discretion, resource the testing to support it, and count the deaths from decline alongside the deaths from infection.

I do not accept the framing that farmers are opposed to environmental measures; the farmers I represent are, on the whole, willing to change practice where the alternative is workable and the transition is funded. What they object to, and what I object to on their behalf, is being asked to bear the cost of the transition personally while the benefit is described as national. If the country wants a different agricultural model, the country can pay for it. That is what every other sector receives when it is asked to restructure, and there is no reason agriculture should be the exception. The specific measure before us fails on its own terms in any case. It does not change behaviour, because there is no alternative fuel for the machinery in question and none is coming to market at scale within the relevant period. A tax that cannot change behaviour is purely a revenue measure, and the Minister should have the honesty to describe it as one rather than dressing it in climate language.

Not a blame exercise, which would be useless and would ensure that nobody ever gives candid advice again, but a serious examination of which measures worked, which did not, and what the costs were, including the costs we did not measure at the time because they were harder to count than the ones we did. But I want to address the charge directly, because it has been made more than once in this debate and it deserves an answer rather than a dismissal. The suggestion is that by legislating here on matters ordinarily devolved, this House is overriding the settlement. I understand why it is made. My answer is that the alternative on offer is not devolved decision-making; it is no decision-making. When the institutions are not sitting, the choice is not between a decision taken in Belfast and a decision taken here. It is between a decision taken here and a vacuum in which public services deteriorate and in which obligations, including international obligations that bind the United Kingdom as a whole, go unmet. I would far rather these matters were settled by an Executive and an Assembly, and everything I have done has been directed at bringing that about. But I am not prepared to say that in the absence of those institutions nothing may be done at all, because the people affected did not choose the impasse and should not bear its whole cost. I would say the same to anyone who suggests that intervention here is a preference rather than a last resort. It is not a preference. It consumes an enormous amount of time, it satisfies nobody, and it makes the eventual restoration of the institutions harder rather than easier, because it creates a habit. That is precisely why I have resisted it as long as I have and why the legislation before us is drawn as narrowly as it is. It addresses what cannot wait and leaves everything else for a restored Executive, which I continue to believe is achievable within a reasonable period if the will exists.
